code.title: Segment tree: range sum with point update
code.python:
# Each node k stores the sum of its range [l, r]
def build(a, t, k, l, r):
    if l == r:
        t[k] = a[l]
        return
    m = (l + r) // 2
    build(a, t, 2 * k, l, m)
    build(a, t, 2 * k + 1, m + 1, r)
    t[k] = t[2 * k] + t[2 * k + 1]

# Point update: walk down to one leaf, then fix the sums on the way back
def update(t, k, l, r, i, v):
    if l == r:
        t[k] = v
        return
    m = (l + r) // 2
    if i <= m:
        update(t, 2 * k, l, m, i, v)
    else:
        update(t, 2 * k + 1, m + 1, r, i, v)
    t[k] = t[2 * k] + t[2 * k + 1]

def query(t, k, l, r, ql, qr):
    if qr < l or r < ql:
        return 0                 # no overlap: identity for sum
    if ql <= l and r <= qr:
        return t[k]              # fully inside: use stored sum
    m = (l + r) // 2
    return query(t, 2 * k, l, m, ql, qr) + query(t, 2 * k + 1, m + 1, r, ql, qr)

a = [2, 1, 5, 3, 4]
n = len(a)
t = [0] * (4 * n)
build(a, t, 1, 0, n - 1)
print("a =", a)
print("sum(1..3) =", query(t, 1, 0, n - 1, 1, 3))
update(t, 1, 0, n - 1, 2, 10)
print("set a[2] = 10")
print("sum(1..3) =", query(t, 1, 0, n - 1, 1, 3))
print("sum(0..4) =", query(t, 1, 0, n - 1, 0, 4))
# Time: build O(N), update and query O(log N). Space: O(N) (4N cells).

followUps:
A segment tree works for any operation that is associative and has an identity value. Associative means the grouping does not matter: (a ⊕ b) ⊕ c = a ⊕ (b ⊕ c), so a node may combine its two halves in any grouping. The identity is what a node outside the query returns: 0 for sum, +∞ for min, −∞ for max, 0 for gcd and xor, 1 for product, the identity matrix for matrix product.

The operation does not need to be commutative (string concatenation works if you always merge left then right) and does not need an inverse (min has none). Example: gcd of [12, 18, 8] = gcd(gcd(12, 18), 8) = gcd(6, 8) = 2. Averages or medians fail directly, but an average works if the node stores the pair (sum, count). Cost stays O(log N) merges per query.

Keep a max segment tree and walk down from the root, always trying the left child first. If a node's max is below x, nothing inside can qualify, so skip it; otherwise go left, and go right only if the left side had no answer.

int first(int k, int l, int r, int x) {
  if (mx[k] < x) return -1;
  if (l == r) return l;
  int m = (l + r) / 2;
  int res = first(2*k, l, m, x);
  return res != -1 ? res : first(2*k+1, m+1, r, x);
}

Example: a = [2, 1, 5, 3, 4], x = 3. Root max is 5, the left half [0..2] has max 5, inside it [0..1] has max 2 (skip), so the answer is index 2. The left call returns −1 at once when its max is too small, so one root-to-leaf path is followed: O(log N) time, O(log N) stack. To search only from index l onward, add a range check and it becomes O(log N) as well.

code.title: Lazy propagation: range add and range sum
code.python:
# Fully covered node: fix its sum now, remember what the children still owe
def apply(k, length, v):
    total[k] += v * length
    lazy[k] += v

# Push the pending tag to both children before going below this node
def push(k, l, r):
    if lazy[k] == 0:
        return
    m = (l + r) // 2
    apply(2 * k, m - l + 1, lazy[k])
    apply(2 * k + 1, r - m, lazy[k])
    lazy[k] = 0

def add(k, l, r, ql, qr, v):
    if qr < l or r < ql:
        return
    if ql <= l and r <= qr:
        apply(k, r - l + 1, v)
        return
    push(k, l, r)
    m = (l + r) // 2
    add(2 * k, l, m, ql, qr, v)
    add(2 * k + 1, m + 1, r, ql, qr, v)
    total[k] = total[2 * k] + total[2 * k + 1]   # pull: rebuild from children

def query(k, l, r, ql, qr):
    if qr < l or r < ql:
        return 0
    if ql <= l and r <= qr:
        return total[k]
    push(k, l, r)
    m = (l + r) // 2
    return query(2 * k, l, m, ql, qr) + query(2 * k + 1, m + 1, r, ql, qr)

a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
n = len(a)
total = [0] * (4 * n)
lazy = [0] * (4 * n)
for i in range(n):
    add(1, 0, n - 1, i, i, a[i])
print("a =", a)
add(1, 0, n - 1, 1, 4, 10)
print("add 10 to [1..4]")
print("sum(0..5) =", query(1, 0, n - 1, 0, 5))
print("sum(2..3) =", query(1, 0, n - 1, 2, 3))
add(1, 0, n - 1, 3, 5, 5)
print("add 5 to [3..5]")
print("sum(3..5) =", query(1, 0, n - 1, 3, 5))
print("sum(0..2) =", query(1, 0, n - 1, 0, 2))
# Time: O(log N) per range update and per query. Space: O(N).

followUps:
Use one tag with three fields: hasSet, setVal and add, read as "first assign setVal to every element (only if hasSet), then add add". Two rules make it work.

  • A new assign x wipes the past: tag becomes (true, x, 0) and sum = x·len.
  • A new add v stacks on top: add += v and sum += v·len; a pending assign stays.

When pushing to a child, send the assign first and the add second. Example on a node of length 3: assign 7 then add 2 gives tag (true, 7, 2) and sum 27; then assign 4 gives (true, 4, 0) and sum 12. Use a boolean, not 0, for "no assign", because 0 is a legal value. Every operation stays O(log N) with O(N) memory.

"Replace every a[i] in [l, r] by ⌊√a[i]⌋" cannot be done lazily, because the new sum cannot be worked out from the old sum. Sums 16 + 9 = 25 and 24 + 1 = 25 are equal, yet after the square root they are 4 + 3 = 7 and 4 + 1 = 5. A tag is only useful when the node's value can be fixed without looking at its children. The same is true for "a[i] = a[i] mod x".

The fix is to go down to the leaves, but stop early where nothing can change. Store max beside sum. For square root, skip any node with max ≤ 1. For mod x, skip any node with max < x. A value reaches 1 after about 6 square roots (for values up to 1018), and each real mod at least halves a value, so the total work is O((N log log V + Q) log N) for square root and O((N + Q) log V · log N) for mod.

code.title: Fenwick tree: point add and range sum in about 10 lines
code.python:
a = [3, 2, -1, 6, 5, 4]
n = len(a)
tree = [0] * (n + 1)   # 1-based, N + 1 cells

# Add v at position i: climb to every box that covers i
def add(i, v):
    while i <= n:
        tree[i] += v
        i += i & -i

# Sum of positions 1..i: jump down by the lowest set bit
def prefix(i):
    s = 0
    while i > 0:
        s += tree[i]
        i -= i & -i
    return s

# A range answer needs subtraction, so the operation must be invertible
def range_sum(l, r):
    return prefix(r) - prefix(l - 1)

for i in range(n):
    add(i + 1, a[i])
print("a =", a, "(positions 1..6)")
print("sum(2..5) =", range_sum(2, 5))
add(3, 3)
print("add 3 at position 3")
print("sum(2..5) =", range_sum(2, 5))
print("prefix(6) =", prefix(6))
# Time: O(log N) per add and per prefix. Space: O(N).

followUps:
Yes, but only when values never go down and you only ask about prefixes. The update must be "raise a[i] to at least v": then every box that covers i can simply take max(tree[j], v), and prefixMax(i) takes the max over the usual boxes.

It breaks in two cases. First, a range [l, r] with l > 1 cannot be answered, because max has no inverse: knowing max(1..r) = 9 and max(1..l−1) = 9 tells you nothing about max(l..r). Second, lowering a value is not possible, because a box does not remember its second largest value. Example: a = [3, 7, 2]; prefixMax(3) = 7. Lowering a[2] to 1 should give 3, but the box only stored 7.

This limited form is enough for longest increasing subsequence: dp values only grow and you ask for the best dp among smaller values. O(log N) per operation, O(N) space.

Keep two Fenwick trees over the difference array d, where adding v to [l, r] means d[l] += v and d[r+1] −= v. One tree stores d[k], the other stores k·d[k].

Derivation: a[j] is the sum of d[1..j], so the prefix sum is P(i) = Σj≤i Σk≤j d[k]. Each d[k] is counted once for every j from k to i, that is (i − k + 1) times. So P(i) = (i + 1)·Σ d[k] − Σ k·d[k].

void rangeAdd(int l, int r, long v) {
  B1.add(l, v);     B1.add(r + 1, -v);
  B2.add(l, v * l); B2.add(r + 1, -v * (r + 1));
}
long prefix(int i) { return (i + 1) * B1.sum(i) - B2.sum(i); }

Check: start with zeros and add 5 to [2, 4]. P(3) = 4·5 − 10 = 10 (two elements of 5). P(5) = 6·0 − (10 − 25) = 15. Range sum is P(r) − P(l − 1). O(log N) per operation, 2N memory.

code.title: Lowest set bit i & -i and the cells a Fenwick tree visits
code.python:
# -i is ~i + 1 in two's complement, so only the lowest 1 bit survives the AND
def lowbit(i):
    return i & -i

samples = [12, 10, 8, 7]
for i in samples:
    print("i = " + str(i) + " (" + bin(i)[2:] + ")  lowbit = " + str(lowbit(i)))

# Prefix query: keep removing the lowest set bit until i becomes 0
q = ""
i = 13
while i > 0:
    q += " " + str(i)
    i -= lowbit(i)
print("prefix(13) reads cells:" + q)

# Point update: keep adding the lowest set bit until i passes n
n = 16
u = ""
i = 5
while i <= n:
    u += " " + str(i)
    i += lowbit(i)
print("update(5) with n = 16 writes cells:" + u)
# Each loop runs at most log2(N) + 1 times. Time: O(log N). Space: O(1).

followUps:
Calling prefix(0) is harmless: the loop does not run and it returns 0, which is the right answer for an empty prefix. The real dangers are index 0 in the update loop and a negative index in the query loop.

  • Update at 0: 0 & −0 = 0, so i += i & −i never moves and the loop runs forever. That is why the tree is 1-based: with 0-based data, call add(i + 1, v).
  • Query at −1: with 0-based indices, prefix(l − 1) for l = 0 passes −1. With while (i != 0) the loop enters and reads tree[−1], which is an out-of-bounds error (or garbage in C++). With while (i > 0) it returns 0 safely.

So write i > 0, and shift indices by one at the entry of both functions. A pure 0-based version also exists: query uses i = (i & (i + 1)) − 1, update uses i |= i + 1.

Store counts in the tree (tree position = value, content = how many times it occurs) and walk down by powers of two, from the largest to 1. At each step, try to jump: if the box just after the current position holds fewer than k items, the answer is beyond it, so take the jump and subtract its count.

int kth(int k) {
  int pos = 0;
  for (int pw = HIGHEST_POW2; pw > 0; pw >>= 1)
    if (pos + pw <= n && tree[pos + pw] < k) { pos += pw; k -= tree[pos]; }
  return pos + 1;
}

It works because tree[pos + pw] covers exactly positions pos+1 .. pos+pw. Example: counts for values 1..8 are [1, 0, 2, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0] and k = 3. tree[8] = 4 (not below 3), tree[4] = 3 (no), tree[2] = 1 < 3 so pos = 2, k = 2; tree[3] = 2 (no). Answer 3, and the sorted items are 1, 3, 3, 6. One pass: O(log N), instead of O(log² N) for binary search over prefix sums.

code.title: Count the nodes a range query visits and compare with 4 log N
code.python:
visited = 0

# Same shape as a real query, but it only counts the nodes it enters
def query(l, r, ql, qr):
    global visited
    visited += 1
    if qr < l or r < ql:
        return                    # disjoint: stop
    if ql <= l and r <= qr:
        return                    # fully covered: stop
    m = (l + r) // 2              # partial: only these nodes go deeper
    query(l, m, ql, qr)
    query(m + 1, r, ql, qr)

for n in [8, 64, 1024, 1048576]:
    log = 0
    while (1 << log) < n:
        log += 1
    visited = 0
    # [1, n-2] is a worst case: both ends cut nodes on every level
    query(0, n - 1, 1, n - 2)
    print("N = " + str(n) + "  query [1, " + str(n - 2) + "]  visited = " + str(visited)
          + "  bound 4*log2(N)+1 = " + str(4 * log + 1))
# Time: O(log N) per query, at most 4 nodes per level. Space: O(log N) stack.

followUps:
Yes, and the bound is even smaller: the bottom-up query reads at most 2 nodes per level, so about 2·log₂ N nodes in total. The loop moves both borders up one level per step (l >>= 1, r >>= 1), and on each level it takes at most one node at the left border (when l is a right child) and one at the right border.

Example with N = 8, leaves at 8..15, query [1, 6], so l = 9 and r = 15 (exclusive). Level 3: take node 9, take node 14. Then l = 5, r = 7. Level 2: take node 5, take node 6. Then l = r = 3 and the loop stops. That is 4 nodes read, while the recursive query enters 11 nodes for the same range. There is also no recursion, so the extra space is O(1). The proof is simpler too: the loop runs at most ⌈log₂ N⌉ + 1 times and does O(1) work each time.

A point update touches exactly one node on each level: the leaf and all its ancestors up to the root. That is the height of the tree plus one, at most ⌈log₂ N⌉ + 1 nodes.

Reason: nodes on one level have ranges that do not overlap, so only one of them contains index i. The recursion never branches; at each node it goes left or right, not both. Example with N = 8 and i = 5: the nodes are [0..7], [4..7], [4..5], [5..5], which is 4 = log₂ 8 + 1. In the bottom-up layout the same path is 13 → 6 → 3 → 1.

For N = 106 that is 21 nodes per update. Time O(log N); the recursive version uses O(log N) stack and the bottom-up version uses O(1) extra space. Compare with a query, which may enter up to about 4 nodes per level.

code.title: Largest node index a recursive segment tree really uses
code.python:
nodes = 0
max_index = 0

# Walk the same recursion as build(): root is 1, children are 2k and 2k+1
def walk(k, l, r):
    global nodes, max_index
    nodes += 1
    if k > max_index:
        max_index = k
    if l == r:
        return
    m = (l + r) // 2
    walk(2 * k, l, m)
    walk(2 * k + 1, m + 1, r)

for n in [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 100, 1000]:
    nodes = 0
    max_index = 0
    walk(1, 0, n - 1)
    # Only 2N-1 nodes exist, but the numbering leaves holes when N is not a power of two
    print("N = " + str(n) + "  nodes = " + str(nodes) + "  max index = " + str(max_index)
          + "  2N = " + str(2 * n) + "  4N = " + str(4 * n))
# The max index is always below 4N, so an array of 4N cells is safe.
# Time: O(N) for the walk. Space: O(log N) stack.

followUps:
It is never worse, and it saves the most when N is equal to or just below a power of two. Let P be the smallest power of two that is ≥ N. The recursive tree has depth ⌈log₂ N⌉, so every index is below 2P, and since P < 2N we always have 2P < 4N.

NP2P4N
1000102420484000
1024102420484096
1025204840964100

So for N = 1000 you save almost half, and for N = 1025 almost nothing. People still write 4N because it needs no loop to find P and is impossible to get wrong in an interview. Use 2P when memory is tight (for example several arrays of 106 nodes with lazy tags), or when you pad the array to length P to get a perfect tree, which also makes bottom-up code simpler.

Keep two partial answers instead of one: resL for pieces taken at the left border and resR for pieces taken at the right border, and always merge in left-to-right order.

T resL = ID, resR = ID;
for (l += n, r += n + 1; l < r; l >>= 1, r >>= 1) {
  if ((l & 1) == 1) resL = merge(resL, t[l++]);   // append on the right
  if ((r & 1) == 1) resR = merge(t[--r], resR);   // put in front
}
return merge(resL, resR);

Pieces from the left border arrive in increasing position, so each new one goes after resL. Pieces from the right border arrive in decreasing position, so each new one goes before resR. Example with string concatenation over [a, b, c, d, e] and query [1, 3]: resL collects "b", resR collects "d" and then "c" + "d", and the result is "bcd". Internal nodes must be built as merge(t[2i], t[2i+1]). Still O(log N).

code.title: Sparse table: O(1) range minimum with two overlapping windows
code.python:
a = [5, 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 6]
n = len(a)
# lg[x] = floor(log2(x)), filled without floating point
lg = [0] * (n + 1)
for i in range(2, n + 1):
    lg[i] = lg[i // 2] + 1
levels = lg[n] + 1
# st[k][i] = min of the 2^k elements starting at i
st = [[0] * n for _ in range(levels)]
st[0] = a[:]
for k in range(1, levels):
    i = 0
    while i + (1 << k) <= n:
        st[k][i] = min(st[k - 1][i], st[k - 1][i + (1 << (k - 1))])
        i += 1

print("a =", a)
queries = [(0, 3), (2, 5), (5, 6), (3, 3), (0, 6)]
for l, r in queries:
    k = lg[r - l + 1]
    # Two windows of length 2^k: they overlap, which is fine because min(x, x) = x
    ans = min(st[k][l], st[k][r - (1 << k) + 1])
    print("min(" + str(l) + ".." + str(r) + ") = " + str(ans) + "  (window length " + str(1 << k) + ")")
# Time: build O(N log N), query O(1). Space: O(N log N). No updates.

followUps:
Cut the array into blocks of about log₂ N elements and build the sparse table only over the block minimums. There are N / log N blocks and log N levels, so the table needs O(N) cells instead of O(N log N).

  • Query covering several blocks: minimum of a suffix of the first block, a prefix of the last block (both precomputed arrays, O(N)), and the sparse table over the whole blocks between them.
  • Query inside one block: for each position store a bit mask of the monotonic stack (which earlier positions in the block are still "smaller than everything after them"). The answer is found with one mask and one lowest-set-bit operation, so it is O(1).

Example: N = 106. A plain table has 20 × 106 ints (80 MB). With blocks of 20 there are 50,000 blocks × 16 levels = 800,000 ints, plus three arrays of N. Build O(N), query O(1).

Turn the tree into an array with an Euler tour, and the lowest common ancestor becomes "the shallowest node between two positions".

  1. Run a DFS and write down a node every time you enter it or come back to it: 2N − 1 entries. Store each entry's depth and first[v], the first position of v.
  2. Build a sparse table over the depths (store the position of the minimum).
  3. LCA(u, v) = the node at the minimum depth between first[u] and first[v].

Example: node 1 has children 2 and 3; node 2 has children 4 and 5. Tour: 1 2 4 2 5 2 1 3 1, depths: 0 1 2 1 2 1 0 1 0. For 4 and 5 the positions are 2 and 4, the minimum depth there is 1 at node 2, so LCA = 2. For 4 and 3 the positions are 2 and 7, minimum depth 0, so LCA = 1. It works because the walk from u to v must pass through their LCA and never goes above it. Build O(N log N), query O(1).

code.title: Mo's algorithm: distinct values in each range, answered offline
code.python:
a = [1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 2, 4, 1]
qs = [(0, 4), (2, 6), (1, 3), (5, 7), (0, 7)]
B = 3   # block size, about sqrt(N)
# Sort by block of l, then by r: r only moves forward inside a block
order = sorted(range(len(qs)), key=lambda i: (qs[i][0] // B, qs[i][1]))

freq = [0] * 5
ans = [0] * len(qs)
cur_l, cur_r, distinct, moves = 0, -1, 0, 0

def add(i):
    global distinct, moves
    freq[a[i]] += 1
    if freq[a[i]] == 1:
        distinct += 1
    moves += 1

def remove(i):
    global distinct, moves
    freq[a[i]] -= 1
    if freq[a[i]] == 0:
        distinct -= 1
    moves += 1

for qid in order:
    l, r = qs[qid]
    # Grow the window first, then shrink it; each step is O(1)
    while cur_l > l:
        cur_l -= 1
        add(cur_l)
    while cur_r < r:
        cur_r += 1
        add(cur_r)
    while cur_l < l:
        remove(cur_l)
        cur_l += 1
    while cur_r > r:
        remove(cur_r)
        cur_r -= 1
    ans[qid] = distinct   # store by original index

print("a =", a)
for i, (l, r) in enumerate(qs):
    print("distinct(" + str(l) + ".." + str(r) + ") = " + str(ans[i]))
print("pointer moves =", moves)
# Time: O((N + Q) * sqrt(N)) plus the sort. Space: O(N + Q).

followUps:
Add a third coordinate, time = how many updates have been applied, and move three pointers instead of two. Each query remembers (l, r, t) where t is the number of updates that came before it.

  • Sort queries by (block of l, block of r, t) with block size B ≈ N2/3.
  • To move time forward, apply update number t: if its position is inside the current window, remove the old value and add the new one; then swap the old and new value in the update record, so the same code undoes it when time moves back.

Cost: l and r each move at most B per query, and t moves at most (number of updates) for each of the (N/B)² pairs of blocks. With B = N2/3 the total is O(N5/3). For N = Q = 105, B is about 2,150 and the work is about 2·108 simple steps, which is fine. It is still offline: all queries and updates must be known first.

A sweep with a Fenwick tree is better whenever each position can add a fixed contribution that depends only on the right end of the query. Then you sort queries by r, move i from left to right, update the tree, and answer every query ending at i with one range sum.

Typical cases: number of distinct values (a 1 at the last occurrence of each value), number of elements ≤ x in a range (sort by x instead), sum of values that appear for the first time, counting pairs with a fixed pattern.

Cost: O((N + Q) log N) against O(N·√Q) for Mo. For N = Q = 105 that is about 3·106 tree steps against about 3·107 window moves, and the sweep code is shorter. Mo is still the right tool when the answer does not split into per-position contributions but add/remove is O(1), for example the sum of (frequency)² in the range or the number of equal pairs.

code.title: Lazy tree with two tags: range assign, range add, range sum
code.python:
a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
n, e = len(a), len(a) - 1   # size and last index
total = [0] * (4 * n)
set_val = [0] * (4 * n)
add = [0] * (4 * n)
has_set = [False] * (4 * n)   # a flag, because 0 is a legal value to assign
# Tag meaning: first assign set_val (if has_set), then add "add"
def apply_set(k, length, x):
    total[k], has_set[k], set_val[k], add[k] = x * length, True, x, 0

def apply_add(k, length, v):
    total[k] += v * length
    add[k] += v

def push(k, l, r):
    m = (l + r) // 2
    # Order matters: the assignment goes down first, then the add
    if has_set[k]:
        apply_set(2 * k, m - l + 1, set_val[k])
        apply_set(2 * k + 1, r - m, set_val[k])
        has_set[k] = False
    if add[k] != 0:
        apply_add(2 * k, m - l + 1, add[k])
        apply_add(2 * k + 1, r - m, add[k])
        add[k] = 0

def update(k, l, r, ql, qr, assign, x):
    if qr < l or r < ql:
        return
    if ql <= l and r <= qr:
        (apply_set if assign else apply_add)(k, r - l + 1, x)
        return
    push(k, l, r)
    m = (l + r) // 2
    update(2 * k, l, m, ql, qr, assign, x)
    update(2 * k + 1, m + 1, r, ql, qr, assign, x)
    total[k] = total[2 * k] + total[2 * k + 1]

def query(k, l, r, ql, qr):
    if qr < l or r < ql:
        return 0
    if ql <= l and r <= qr:
        return total[k]
    push(k, l, r)
    m = (l + r) // 2
    return query(2 * k, l, m, ql, qr) + query(2 * k + 1, m + 1, r, ql, qr)

for i in range(n):
    update(1, 0, e, i, i, True, a[i])
print("a =", a)
update(1, 0, e, 1, 3, True, 7)
print("assign 7 to [1..3] -> sum(0..4) =", query(1, 0, e, 0, 4))
update(1, 0, e, 2, 4, False, 2)
print("add 2 to [2..4]    -> sum(0..4) =", query(1, 0, e, 0, 4))
print("sum(2..3) =", query(1, 0, e, 2, 3))
update(1, 0, e, 0, 1, True, 0)
print("assign 0 to [0..1] -> sum(0..4) =", query(1, 0, e, 0, 4))
update(1, 0, e, 0, 4, False, 1)
print("add 1 to [0..4]    -> sum(0..2) =", query(1, 0, e, 0, 2))
# Time: O(log N) per operation. Space: O(N).

followUps:
Very little changes: add one more field mn to every node, and the tags stay exactly the same. Both updates change the minimum in a predictable way, so a fully covered node can still be fixed in O(1).

  • assign x: mn = x (and sum = x·len).
  • add v: mn += v (and sum += v·len).
  • pull: mn = min(mn of left, mn of right).
  • query: return +∞ for a node outside the range, not 0.

Example: a node covers [7, 9, 9] with mn = 7, sum = 25. Add 2 gives mn = 9, sum = 31. Assign 4 gives mn = 4, sum = 12. The common mistake is to reuse 0 as the "outside" value for the min query. Time stays O(log N) per operation; memory grows by one array. Max works the same way, and with min stored you can also search for the first element below a limit.

Use one tag (b, c) that means "replace x by b·x + c", all modulo p. The "nothing pending" tag is (1, 0). Every update is a special case: add v = (1, v), multiply by m = (m, 0), assign x = (0, x), so no boolean flag is needed.

  • Apply to a node: sum = (b·sum + c·len) mod p.
  • Compose a new tag (b2, c2) on top of an old tag (b1, c1): b2·(b1·x + c1) + c2, so the result is (b2·b1, b2·c1 + c2).

Check with old (2, 3) and new (5, 1): the composed tag is (10, 16). For x = 1: first 2·1 + 3 = 5, then 5·5 + 1 = 26, and 10·1 + 16 = 26. The order matters: composing the other way would give (10, 8), which is wrong. Use 64-bit numbers and take mod after every multiplication, because two values below 109 multiply to about 1018. O(log N) per operation.

code.title: Persistent segment tree: k-th smallest in a[l..r], online
code.python:
from bisect import bisect_left

a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]
n = len(a)
vals = sorted(set(a))   # rank -> value
m = len(vals)
# left child, right child, count of values in the node's rank range
L = [0] * (n * 20)
R = [0] * (n * 20)
C = [0] * (n * 20)
cnt = 0                 # node 0 is the empty tree

# Make a new version: copy only the path to "pos", share everything else
def insert(prev, l, r, pos):
    global cnt
    cnt += 1
    cur = cnt
    L[cur], R[cur], C[cur] = L[prev], R[prev], C[prev] + 1
    if l < r:
        mid = (l + r) // 2
        if pos <= mid:
            L[cur] = insert(L[prev], l, mid, pos)
        else:
            R[cur] = insert(R[prev], mid + 1, r, pos)
    return cur

# Walk version u (before l) and version v (up to r) together
def kth(u, v, l, r, k):
    if l == r:
        return l
    mid = (l + r) // 2
    in_left = C[L[v]] - C[L[u]]   # how many values of a[l..r] have a small rank
    if k <= in_left:
        return kth(L[u], L[v], l, mid, k)
    return kth(R[u], R[v], mid + 1, r, k - in_left)

root = [0] * (n + 1)
for i in range(n):
    root[i + 1] = insert(root[i], 0, m - 1, bisect_left(vals, a[i]))
print("a =", a)
for l, r, k in [(0, 4, 2), (2, 6, 3), (0, 7, 5), (5, 7, 1)]:
    rank = kth(root[l], root[r + 1], 0, m - 1, k)
    print("k = " + str(k) + " smallest in a[" + str(l) + ".." + str(r) + "] = " + str(vals[rank]))
print("nodes created =", cnt)
# Time: O(N log N) build, O(log N) per query. Space: O(N log N) nodes.

followUps:
About 1.8 million nodes, which is roughly 22 MB with three 4-byte fields per node. Each insertion copies one root-to-leaf path. With 105 distinct ranks the tree has ⌈log₂ 105⌉ = 17 levels below the root, so a path has 18 nodes.

Count: 105 insertions × 18 nodes = 1.8·106 nodes. Each node holds left child, right child and count: 12 bytes, so 21.6 MB. In practice people allocate N × 20 = 2·106 nodes (24 MB) to be safe. Node 0 can act as the empty tree whose children are itself, so no separate base tree is needed.

Compare with the naive idea of one full tree per prefix: 105 trees × 2·105 nodes = 2·1010 nodes, which is impossible. Sharing untouched subtrees is what makes it O(N log N). Use arrays of ints rather than objects; in Java an object per node would cost several times more.

Yes, but not with the simple chain of versions, because changing a[i] would change every version from i to N. The standard fix is a Fenwick tree of segment trees: Fenwick cell j owns a value-count segment tree (created on demand) for the positions that cell covers.

  • Update a[i] = v: for each of the log N Fenwick cells that cover i, subtract 1 at the old rank and add 1 at the new rank. O(log² N) time and new nodes.
  • Query k-th in [l, r]: collect the log N roots for prefix r (plus) and for prefix l − 1 (minus), then walk all of them down together, summing left-child counts. O(log² N).

Memory is O((N + Q) log² N) nodes: tens of millions for N = Q = 105, which is heavy. If memory is tight, use sqrt decomposition with a sorted copy of each block, or solve offline with parallel binary search and one Fenwick tree in O(N) memory.

code.title: Range square-root update without lazy tags: stop where max <= 1
code.python:
a = [16, 81, 1, 100, 7, 4]
n = len(a)
total = [0] * (4 * n)
mx = [0] * (4 * n)
leaf_visits = 0

def isqrt(x):
    r = 0
    while (r + 1) * (r + 1) <= x:
        r += 1
    return r

def pull(k):
    total[k] = total[2 * k] + total[2 * k + 1]
    mx[k] = max(mx[2 * k], mx[2 * k + 1])

def build(k, l, r):
    if l == r:
        total[k] = mx[k] = a[l]
        return
    m = (l + r) // 2
    build(2 * k, l, m)
    build(2 * k + 1, m + 1, r)
    pull(k)

def sqrt_range(k, l, r, ql, qr):
    global leaf_visits
    # Prune: if every value here is 0 or 1, a square root changes nothing
    if qr < l or r < ql or mx[k] <= 1:
        return
    if l == r:
        total[k] = mx[k] = isqrt(total[k])
        leaf_visits += 1
        return
    m = (l + r) // 2
    sqrt_range(2 * k, l, m, ql, qr)
    sqrt_range(2 * k + 1, m + 1, r, ql, qr)
    pull(k)

def query(k, l, r, ql, qr):
    if qr < l or r < ql:
        return 0
    if ql <= l and r <= qr:
        return total[k]
    m = (l + r) // 2
    return query(2 * k, l, m, ql, qr) + query(2 * k + 1, m + 1, r, ql, qr)

build(1, 0, n - 1)
print("a = " + str(a) + "  sum = " + str(query(1, 0, n - 1, 0, n - 1)))
for l, r in [(0, 3), (0, 5), (0, 5), (0, 5)]:
    sqrt_range(1, 0, n - 1, l, r)
    print("sqrt on [" + str(l) + ".." + str(r) + "] -> sum = " + str(query(1, 0, n - 1, 0, n - 1))
          + "  leaf visits so far = " + str(leaf_visits))
# Each value shrinks to 1 after about log log V square roots, then is skipped.
# Time: O((N log log V + Q) log N) in total. Space: O(N).

followUps:
The key fact is that a real mod at least halves the number: if x ≤ a, then a mod x < a / 2. So one element can be changed at most log₂ V times before it becomes smaller than every x.

Proof of the fact: the remainder is smaller than x, and it is also at most a − x (we subtract x at least once). So a mod x < min(x, a − x + 1), and the smaller of x and a − x is at most a / 2. Examples: 100 mod 60 = 40, 100 mod 30 = 10, 100 mod 51 = 49; all below 50.

Algorithm: store max per node and skip any node with max < x, because nothing in it changes. Every leaf we do reach is halved, so there are at most N·log₂ V leaf changes in total, each costing O(log N) on the path. A point assignment can raise one value again, which adds at most log₂ V more changes per assignment. Total: O((N + Q) · log V · log N).

For the update "a[i] = min(a[i], x) on [l, r]" with range sum, each node stores four things: the max, the strict second max, the count of the max, and the sum. They let the node be fixed in O(1) whenever only its largest value changes.

  • x ≥ max: nothing changes, stop.
  • second max < x < max: only the max elements drop to x, so sum −= cnt·(max − x), max = x, leave a tag, stop.
  • x ≤ second max: go into the children.

Example: a node holds [5, 5, 3, 1] with max 5, count 2, second max 3, sum 14. For x = 4 the middle case applies: sum = 14 − 2·1 = 12. For x = 2 we must go down. Going down is paid for because it makes two different values in that node equal, and the number of different values can only shrink so many times. The amortized cost is O(log N) per operation for chmin alone, and O(log² N) when range add is mixed in.

code.title: Coordinate compression: Fenwick tree over coordinates up to 10^9

followUps:
At most about 3 million, and usually close to 1.5 million. The range [0, 109] needs ⌈log₂ 109⌉ = 30 halvings, so one point update walks a path of 31 nodes and creates only the ones that are missing.

Simple bound: 105 × 31 = 3.1·106 nodes. Tighter: the top 17 levels have at most 217 ≈ 131,000 nodes in total however many updates there are, so paths share them. Below that each update adds at most 14 new nodes: 105 × 14 + 1.3·105 ≈ 1.5·106.

At 16 bytes per node (two child indices and a 64-bit value) that is 25 to 50 MB. Allocate one array pool of the worst-case size and use int indices instead of pointers. Queries create no nodes if a missing child is treated as "all zeros". Range updates with lazy tags can create up to about 4 × 31 nodes per operation, because pushing a tag creates both children.

The bug is that compression can glue together two coordinates that had a gap between them, so something that is still uncovered in reality looks covered. The classic case is counting visible posters on a wall.

Posters, in order: A = [1, 10], B = [1, 4], C = [6, 10]. In reality cell 5 still shows A, so 3 posters are visible. The endpoints are 1, 4, 6, 10, giving ranks 0, 1, 2, 3. Compressed: A = [0, 3], B = [0, 1], C = [2, 3]. Now B and C together cover all of A, and the program answers 2.

Fix: keep the gaps. Either also add x + 1 for every right end (or one extra coordinate between two neighbours that differ by more than 1), or work with half-open intervals [l, r + 1) and compress l and r + 1. Here that gives 1, 5, 6, 11 and the pieces [1, 5), [5, 6), [6, 11); the middle piece keeps poster A. Cost is unchanged: at most 2 coordinates per interval, O(N log N).

code.title: Zone-map idea: per-block max lets a range scan skip whole blocks
code.python:
# Latency samples; a real store would hold millions per block
a = [12, 40, 7, 33, 95, 18, 22, 5, 61, 30, 44, 9]
n = len(a)
B = 4
# Precompute one summary (the max) per block, like a rollup or zone map
block_max = [0] * ((n + B - 1) // B)
for i in range(n):
    block_max[i // B] = max(block_max[i // B], a[i])

print("a =", a)
print("block max (B = 4) =", block_max)
for l, r in [(2, 10), (0, 11), (8, 9), (1, 6)]:
    best = 0
    reads = 0
    i = l
    while i <= r:
        if i % B == 0 and i + B - 1 <= r:
            best = max(best, block_max[i // B])   # whole block inside: one read
            i += B
        else:
            best = max(best, a[i])                # edge of the range: read the raw value
            i += 1
        reads += 1
    print("max(" + str(l) + ".." + str(r) + ") = " + str(best) + "  reads = " + str(reads)
          + "  (plain scan = " + str(r - l + 1) + ")")
# Time: O(N) to build, O(B + N/B) per query, about sqrt(N) when B = sqrt(N). Space: O(N/B).

followUps:
Start with one reader-writer lock around the whole structure: many range queries can run together, and an update takes the lock alone for only O(log N) steps. This is often enough.

If writers are the bottleneck, there are two steps up.

  • Copy-on-write versions: a writer copies the log N nodes on its path (like a persistent segment tree) and then swaps the root pointer in one atomic step. Readers never lock and always see a complete version. Writers still queue behind each other.
  • Sharding: split the index range into blocks, each with its own lock and its own subtotal. Writers to different blocks do not wait for each other; a query locks only the two edge blocks and reads the totals of the others.

What you must not do is let a reader see a half-finished update: with a sum tree, an update that has changed the leaf but not yet the root makes sum(0..7) disagree with sum(0..3) + sum(4..7).

Because a database reads from disk in pages, and a B-tree node is sized to fill one page, so the tree is very short. A node with a few hundred keys fits in a 4 to 16 KB page; a binary node would waste the page on two children.

Numbers: for 109 rows a binary tree is about 30 levels deep, so about 30 page reads or cache misses per lookup. A B-tree with 256 children per node needs log256 109 ≈ 4 levels, and the top levels stay in memory.

Two more reasons. A B-tree handles inserted and deleted keys by splitting and merging nodes, while a segment tree assumes a fixed range of indices. And the leaves of a B-tree are in sorted order and linked, so a range scan is a sequential read. The segment-tree idea is still used inside: an internal B-tree node can store the count or sum of each child subtree, which gives range aggregates and "k-th row" in O(log N).

code.title: Stress test: random tiny cases, segment tree against brute force
code.python:
seed = 12345

# Small fixed random generator so every run (and every language) sees the same tests
def rnd():
    global seed
    seed = (seed * 75 + 74) % 65537
    return seed

INF = 2147483647   # identity for min, not 0
n = 0
t = []

def update(i, v):
    i += n
    t[i] = v
    while i > 1:
        i >>= 1
        t[i] = min(t[2 * i], t[2 * i + 1])

def query(l, r):   # min of a[l..r], bottom-up tree
    res = INF
    l += n
    r += n + 1
    while l < r:
        if l & 1:
            res = min(res, t[l])
            l += 1
        if r & 1:
            r -= 1
            res = min(res, t[r])
        l >>= 1
        r >>= 1
    return res

tests, checks, mismatches = 300, 0, 0
for test in range(tests):
    n = 1 + rnd() % 8                  # tiny sizes hit the edge cases
    a = [0] * n
    t = [INF] * (2 * n)
    for i in range(n):
        a[i] = rnd() % 100
        update(i, a[i])
    for op in range(10):
        kind = rnd() % 2
        x = rnd() % n
        y = rnd() % n
        if kind == 0:
            v = rnd() % 100
            a[x] = v
            update(x, v)
            continue
        l, r = min(x, y), max(x, y)
        brute = min(a[l:r + 1])        # the obviously correct O(N) answer
        checks += 1
        if brute != query(l, r):
            mismatches += 1
            print("MISMATCH n=" + str(n) + " l=" + str(l) + " r=" + str(r))
print("tests = " + str(tests) + ", sizes 1..8, 10 random operations each")
print("queries checked = " + str(checks) + ", mismatches = " + str(mismatches))
# Time: O(tests * ops * N) for the brute force. Space: O(N).

followUps:
Tiny ones: N from 1 to about 8, with values from a small range such as 0 to 5, and many operations per test. Almost every segment tree bug lives at a boundary, and small cases hit every boundary quickly and give a failing case you can read.

  • N = 1, 2, 3: the leaf case, an empty half, wrong mid split.
  • N = 5, 6, 7: not a power of two, so the tree is uneven and array-size and padding bugs show up.
  • Small values: ties, zeros and repeated values appear often (0 as "no tag" bugs, wrong identity).
  • Queries with l = r and with the full range, and updates that touch the same place twice in a row (tag composition order).

Run about 1,000 tests of 10 to 20 operations; that takes milliseconds. Print the seed or the whole case on the first mismatch. Test overflow separately with a few large values, because a large random test that fails is too big to debug by hand.

Print one line per node, indented by depth, with its range, its value and its pending tag. For N up to 8 that is at most 15 lines and you can check each against a hand calculation.

void dump(int k, int l, int r, int depth) {
  print("  ".repeat(depth) + "[" + l + ".." + r + "] sum=" + sum[k] + " lazy=" + lazy[k]);
  if (l == r) return;
  int m = (l + r) / 2;
  dump(2*k, l, m, depth + 1); dump(2*k+1, m+1, r, depth + 1);
}

What to look for: a parent whose value is not the merge of its children (missing pull), a tag left on a leaf, a node whose range is wrong (mid split differs between functions). For a = [2, 1, 5] the first lines should be [0..2] sum=8, then [0..1] sum=3. A second quick view is the "flattened" array: query every single point and print the N results, which shows what the tree believes the array is. O(N) per dump.

code.title: Distinct values in a range, offline: sweep by r with a Fenwick tree
code.python:
a = [1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 2, 4, 1]
qs = [(0, 4), (2, 6), (1, 3), (5, 7), (0, 7)]
n = len(a)
tree = [0] * (n + 1)

def add(i, v):
    i += 1
    while i <= n:
        tree[i] += v
        i += i & -i

def prefix(i):
    s = 0
    i += 1
    while i > 0:
        s += tree[i]
        i -= i & -i
    return s

# Offline: answer the queries in order of their right end
order = sorted(range(len(qs)), key=lambda i: qs[i][1])
last = [-1] * 5            # last[v] = latest index where value v was seen
ans = [0] * len(qs)
nxt = 0
for i in range(n):
    # Keep a 1 only at the latest occurrence of each value
    if last[a[i]] != -1:
        add(last[a[i]], -1)
    add(i, 1)
    last[a[i]] = i
    # Every query ending here: count the 1s inside [l, i]
    while nxt < len(order) and qs[order[nxt]][1] == i:
        qid = order[nxt]
        nxt += 1
        ans[qid] = prefix(i) - prefix(qs[qid][0] - 1)

print("a =", a)
for i, (l, r) in enumerate(qs):
    print("distinct(" + str(l) + ".." + str(r) + ") = " + str(ans[i]))
# Time: O((N + Q) log N). Space: O(N + Q).

followUps:
Because for a fixed right end r, a value appears in [l, r] exactly when its latest occurrence at or before r is at position ≥ l. So each value gets exactly one mark, at that latest position, and counting marks inside [l, r] counts each present value once and each absent value zero times.

Why not first occurrences? A mark at an early copy could lie left of l even though a later copy is inside the window, so the value would be missed. The latest copy is the one nearest to r, so if any copy is in the window, that one is.

Example: a = [1, 2, 1, 3] and r = 3. Marks are at index 1 (value 2), index 2 (value 1) and index 3 (value 3); index 0 lost its mark when the second 1 arrived. Query [1, 3]: 3 marks, and the values are {2, 1, 3}. Query [3, 3]: 1 mark. Each index gains a mark once and loses it at most once, so the sweep is O((N + Q) log N).

It becomes O(log² N) per update and per query, using a tree inside a tree. The online idea is: count positions i in [l, r] whose previous equal value prev[i] is before l. A point update changes prev at no more than 3 positions: the changed index, the old next copy of its old value, and the next copy of its new value. Keep a sorted set of positions for every value to find them in O(log N).

Then you need "count i in [l, r] with prev[i] < l" while prev values change. Use a Fenwick tree over positions where each cell holds a count structure over prev values (a dynamic segment tree or an order-statistic tree). Each prev change touches log N cells and costs log N in each.

Example: a = [1, 2, 1], prev = [−1, −1, 0]. Set a[1] = 1: prev becomes [−1, 0, 1], so two entries changed. Memory is O((N + Q) log² N) nodes. A lighter option is sqrt blocks with sorted prev values: O(√N · log N) per query.
